The Map and the Garden

Mara kept a notebook beside the greenhouse door. Every evening she wrote down how much water she had given each bed. The notebook was wonderfully neat. The plants were not. One row leaned into the path, another drooped, and the lettuces nearest the door looked as if they had given up on the whole enterprise. She could tell you exactly how many litres she had poured. She could not yet tell you what the plants needed.

Measurement is useful because memory is unreliable. Without a record, yesterday's generous watering becomes today's vague impression. A notebook can interrupt that drift. But a measurement is a description of one part of a situation, not a substitute for understanding the situation. Mara had measured her effort. She had not measured the conditions under which that effort helped.

This distinction matters whenever a convenient number begins to stand for a difficult goal. Counting pages read is easier than noticing whether an argument has changed your mind. Counting meetings is easier than discovering whether a team understands its work. The count is not worthless. It simply cannot carry the whole meaning we ask it to carry.

Consider the greenhouse again. Giving every bed the same amount of water looked fair in the notebook. In the soil it meant something else. The sunny bed dried quickly, while a shaded corner stayed damp. Equal inputs produced unequal conditions. Once Mara began touching the soil before reaching for the watering can, the notebook became useful in a different way: a record she could interpret, rather than a rule she had to obey.

It is tempting to turn this story into a campaign against measurement. That would miss the point. A broken thermometer does not prove that temperature is imaginary, and a poorly chosen count does not make observation unnecessary. The problem begins when an indicator becomes a target so complete that other evidence is treated as an inconvenience.

In other words, measuring an activity and achieving its purpose are not the same thing. We may repeat that sentence because the confusion returns in so many respectable disguises. A school celebrates attendance while students remain bewildered. A support team celebrates the speed with which it closes requests while customers write back with the same unresolved problem. Each number can be accurate, and each interpretation can still be wrong.

There is an important limit to the lesson. Some measurements are closely connected to the outcome that matters. In a controlled process, a well-chosen threshold may be exactly the rule people need. It would be foolish to replace such a rule with someone's passing intuition. The task is to ask what the indicator leaves out, how stable its connection to the goal is, and what evidence would make us revise our confidence in it.

Mara did not throw away the notebook. She added a narrow column for observations: dry beneath the surface, damp near the wall, leaves recovering. None of these notes was a complete explanation. Together they made it harder to mistake a tidy record for a healthy garden. The useful question was no longer whether she had met yesterday's watering quota. It was what she had learned that would help her care for the plants tomorrow.
